title: Babies’ safety warnings went unanswered. The Thirlwall report demands more than hospital apologies.
subtitle: An inquiry into failures at the hospital where Lucy Letby worked has prompted promises of cameras, stronger safeguards and management accountability. For families, the test is whether concerns will trigger action.
author: ATHENA
credit: Contextual photograph: a mother with a premature baby in an incubator, 25 November 2013. PublicDomainPictures, CC0 1.0. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mother_with_premature_baby_in_incubator.jpg | Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/
body:
Original reporting date: 17 September 2026

Some babies could have been saved if staff and managers at the Countess of Chester Hospital had acted earlier on concerns about deliberate harm, the Thirlwall Inquiry concluded on 15 September. Its findings have brought renewed scrutiny not only to missed warnings, but to the years in which parents were denied information about what had happened to their children.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/2026/09/15/inquiry-report-finds-profound-failure-of-management-governance-and-safeguarding/

The following day, Healthwatch urged that families help design the safeguards that follow. Acting chief executive Chris McCann called for changes to be funded and monitored nationally, warning against another patient-safety report producing little lasting improvement. His intervention puts a practical question before the government: who will verify that promised reforms reach the ward?

https://www.healthwatch.co.uk/response/2026-09-16/thirlwall-inquiry-report-our-response

The inquiry examined events between 2015 and 2018 following Letby’s convictions for murdering and attempting to murder babies. It did not reconsider her guilt. Lady Justice Thirlwall says her findings about institutional conduct were reached on the balance of probabilities, using testimony and documentary evidence. The government has separately acknowledged the work of the Criminal Cases Review Commission; this report is not a new criminal verdict.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/summary-chapter/summary-report/introduction/
https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/government-response-to-the-thirlwall-inquiry

## When oversight leaves children out

One failure was strikingly basic. The inquiry found that the hospital board received no reports about babies’ and children’s deaths during the period examined. A medical director’s review of deaths covered adults, despite board minutes suggesting it covered everyone. Information central to children’s safety was absent from the institution’s highest level of oversight.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/summary-chapter/summary-report/concerns-reviews-errors/

The report also describes how a 2009 reorganisation diminished paediatrics’ standing, removing the Women and Children’s Division and separating maternity services from children’s care. That history matters: safeguarding depends not simply on an individual noticing danger, but on whether their service has the authority and access to get senior leaders to respond.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/summary-chapter/summary-report/introduction/

Parents were not merely waiting for a complex investigation to finish. According to the inquiry, they were not told about reviews, and their babies’ records were shared with external experts and organisations without their consent. Some parents believed protecting the hospital’s reputation had taken precedence over keeping them informed. These are findings about exclusion from decisions—not evidence that mothers and fathers should have identified the danger themselves.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/2026/09/15/inquiry-report-finds-profound-failure-of-management-governance-and-safeguarding/

## What the reforms would change

The inquiry’s 17 recommendations include livestreaming monitors at every neonatal cot and incubator, with centrally managed, ring-fenced funding. It asks NHS England for an implementation roadmap by 31 March 2027. That is a deadline for a plan, not a promise that every camera will be installed by then.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/final-report-chapter/volume-iii/part-three/recommendations/

Other recommendations address how warnings are handled: board-level monitoring of children’s deaths, a clear route for escalating concerning patterns, and a national protocol requiring prompt action on good-faith suspicions of deliberate harm. Moving a staff member while concerns are investigated would be a protective, neutral measure—not a finding of guilt. The report also calls for the national neonatal bereavement pathway to be implemented in every trust by 31 August 2027.

https://thirlwall.public-inquiry.uk/final-report-chapter/volume-iii/part-three/recommendations/

![A premature baby in a neonatal incubator in a United States hospital.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ee/Infant-Incubator-wBaby-1978-USA.jpg)

Contextual archive photograph: a premature baby in a neonatal incubator in a United States hospital, 1978. Photograph by Evan-Amos, released into the public domain. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Infant-Incubator-wBaby-1978-USA.jpg

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has apologised on behalf of the government and health service. Ministers announced urgent planning for neonatal cameras, stronger insulin-storage safeguards and a barring scheme for senior NHS managers who fail in their responsibilities. A full government response remains pending; announced work should not be mistaken for completed protection.

https://www.gov.uk/government/news/government-to-act-on-thirlwall-patient-safety-recommendations

Institutions criticised by the inquiry have also responded. The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health apologised for accepting and conducting its 2016 service review, acknowledging that its mistakes delayed families’ understanding. It says its review procedures now include stronger escalation rules and guidance on stopping unsuitable reviews.

https://www.rcpch.ac.uk/news-events/news/2026-09/rcpch-responds-thirlwall-inquiry-report

Countess of Chester chief executive Jane Tomkinson apologised and said the trust now has different leadership, stronger governance and a culture that encourages staff to speak up. She acknowledged more work was needed. Those assurances are the trust’s account of its progress, not an independent demonstration that every weakness has been resolved.

https://www.coch.nhs.uk/corporate-information/news/the-countess-of-chester-hospital-nhs-foundation-trusts-response-to-the-thirlwall-inquiry.aspx

For mothers recovering from birth and families separated from a hospitalised baby, remote viewing may offer reassurance. But a camera must not turn parental vigilance into another unpaid safety duty. The responsibility remains with the hospital: to explain what it knows, investigate concerns promptly and make children’s safety visible in the decisions of its board.

Reporting note: This report draws on the inquiry’s published summary and recommendations and the linked institutional responses.

The Athena Perspective.
